problem: Prior Instance ImageGoal Navigation (IIN) methods such as Mod-IIN and IEVE rely on 2D semantic BEV maps. These maps keep occupancy and category but lose 3D geometry and instance-level texture. As a result the agent cannot tell the goal instance apart from same-class distractors from the map alone, and must explore further and verify candidates up close, which hurts path efficiency (SPL).
motivation: IIN requires recognising a specific object instance from a goal image taken with different camera intrinsics, viewpoint and height than the agent's. Semantic-level maps are enough for ObjectNav but not for this instance-level task. The authors observe that 3D Gaussian Splatting stores explicit geometry and appearance and renders novel views quickly. A scene map built this way could synthesise views of every candidate instance and match them against the goal image directly, which would turn IIN into PointGoal navigation.
key_idea: Build a scene-level 'Semantic Gaussian' map (isotropic 3DGS with a semantic label per Gaussian) during a first exploration episode. In later episodes, render each same-class candidate instance, possibly from novel views, and pick the goal instance by keypoint matching against the goal image. Then plan a path to it with FMM on the projected 2D grid.
insight: Most of the gain is in efficiency, and it comes from localising the goal instance before moving, with no in-episode verification. SR improves only modestly over the strongest baseline (72.5 vs 70.5), while SPL jumps from 0.347 to 0.578. The texture-preserving map, rather than the scene memory alone, is what matters: IEVE and Mod-IIN given the same persistent scene map only reach SPL 0.331–0.347 (Table I). The ablations (Table II) show that recognition is the bottleneck. Replacing the classifier with a random category gives 0.375/0.291 SR/SPL; replacing matching with random choice gives 0.444/0.353; a GT match raises SR to 0.850; GT goal localisation raises it to 0.946. Novel-view synthesis helps only slightly (w/o NVS 0.716/0.557), because 3DGS built from few exploration views produces holes and artifacts off-trajectory. Matching success rises 0.811→0.832 with NVS versus 0.846 with GT renders, and nv=5 does not beat nv=3 (Table V). The goal-category classifier mainly buys speed: it cuts matching time by about 2.5x for a 0.039 drop in match success (Table III).
method: Frontier Exploration (first episode per scene): maintain an exploration map and an obstacle map, repeatedly go to the nearest reachable frontier until the floor is covered, and collect RGB-D + pose observations.

Semantic Gaussian representation: isotropic 3D Gaussians with 9 params each (RGB color, 3D mean, radius, opacity, semantic label l). Color is view-independent. Rendering by alpha compositing produces RGB, depth, silhouette and semantic maps.

Semantic Gaussian Construction (SplaTAM-style, known poses): Mask R-CNN segments each frame. New Gaussians are densified where the silhouette is < 0.5 or where GT depth lies in front of the rendered depth with error > 50× the median depth error. Parameters are then optimised by differentiable rendering with RGB, depth and segmentation losses; Gaussians are never pruned.

Goal classifier: a ResNet-50 (ImageNet-pretrained, fine-tuned on HM3D-SEM train-split goal images) predicts which of 6 categories the goal image shows. Only Gaussians/instances of that class are then queried, shrinking the search space.

Match & Grounding: for each candidate instance, take the training view(s) containing it and optionally add novel views by rotating the camera about the object (θ=±15°, ±30°, horizontal/vertical). Extract DISK keypoints, match them to the goal image with LightGlue, and pick the instance with the most matches (argmax over max matches). DBSCAN clusters the instance's Gaussians to reject segmentation outliers and yields the goal position.

Path planning: collapse Gaussians to a point cloud, voxelise, and project to a 2D BEV occupancy grid. The Fast Marching Method computes a distance field to the goal; pick a local waypoint that avoids obstacles and convert it to discrete actions until the goal is reached (runs at >20 FPS).

setting.backbone: Modular, no learned policy: Mask R-CNN segmentation + ResNet-50 goal-image classifier (fine-tuned) + DISK/LightGlue keypoint matching (off-the-shelf) + 3DGS map optimised per scene + FMM planner
setting.training_data: ResNet-50 classifier: ImageNet-pretrained, fine-tuned on goal images from the HM3D-SEM train split (IIN episodes). Mask R-CNN, DISK and LightGlue are used off-the-shelf. The Semantic Gaussian is fitted per scene at test time from the agent's own exploration observations.
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D (640×480, Stretch embodiment, camera at 1.31 m) + sensor pose reading + goal image (512×512, different FOV/height)
setting.action_space: discrete {STOP, FORWARD 0.25 m, TURN_LEFT/TURN_RIGHT 25° as stated in paper}
setting.privileged: Pre-exploration and cross-episode scene memory: frontier exploration in the first episode of each scene builds the Semantic Gaussian, which is reused in all following episodes of that scene. Also uses the sensor pose reading as ground-truth pose for mapping. For poorly reconstructed scenes, the original training views are used instead of NVS renders.

numbers.backbone: Mask R-CNN + ResNet-50 classifier + DISK/LightGlue + Semantic Gaussian (3DGS) map + FMM
numbers.extra: Scene-level map built by pre-exploration in the first episode of each scene and reused across later episodes (the non-scene-map baselines use per-episode maps). Goal classifier fine-tuned on HM3D train goal images.

numbers_note: The evaluation split is not named explicitly. The paper uses the IIN episode dataset (1K val episodes) and says 'On the validation subset, a total of 795 unique object instances have been observed', so the results are assumed to be the HM3D IIN val split. Metrics are printed as fractions (0.725 → 72.5). Additional ablation and oracle rows appear in Table II: w/o Classifier 0.375/0.291, w/o Match 0.444/0.353, w/o NVS 0.716/0.557, SIFT 0.655/0.519, GlueStick 0.723/0.577, GT Match 0.850/0.672, GT Goal Localization 0.946/0.744. Table VI also has a GT-NVS variant at 0.747/0.289. Tables III and V report matching-success rates, not navigation metrics. The FPS comparison and rendering quality (PSNR/MS-SSIM/LPIPS/depth L1 per scene) are shown only in figures (Fig. 7, Fig. 11). The paper does not say whether the exploration episode is counted in the reported metrics.
results: On HM3D IIN, GaussNav reaches SR 0.725 / SPL 0.578. The strongest baseline, IEVE InternImage given a persistent scene map, gets 0.705 / 0.347, so SPL rises by 0.231 while SR rises only 0.020; the original episodic IEVE gets 0.702 / 0.252. End-to-end (OVRL-v2 IIN 0.248 SR) and MultiON-transfer baselines are far behind. GaussNav runs at >20 FPS, the fastest of the modular methods. Without pre-exploration (inside the IEVE framework), the Gaussian map gives only a small gain: 0.723 / 0.265 vs 0.702 / 0.252.
limitations: Needs a full pre-exploration episode per scene and assumes a static scene reused across episodes. Most of the SPL gain depends on this; without pre-exploration the improvement over IEVE is small (SPL 0.265 vs 0.252).

Instance re-identification by keypoint matching and goal grounding remain error-prone: GT matching lifts SR to 0.850 and GT goal location to 0.946. NVS from sparse exploration views produces holes and artifacts, so larger nv does not help.

Reconstruction quality varies strongly by scene, partly due to low-fidelity HM3D textures, and some scenes fall back to raw training views. The setup is closed-set (6 categories, trained classifier), evaluation is simulation only, and each floor is handled separately.
compares_to: IEVE Mask RCNN / InternImage (episodic and scene map)
